spec.title: Card testing
spec.text: Three or more small online authorizations on one card within an hour, followed by a larger purchase: recommend `DECLINE_TRANSACTION` and `STEP_UP_AUTH`. If a purchase over $100 has already cleared, recommend `BLOCK_CARD`.

branches.if: a purchase over $100 has already cleared

tokens.text: If a purchase over $100 has already cleared,

value.clause: a purchase over $100 has already cleared

choices.question: What amount is 'small'?

options.label: under $10.10 (5th percentile of online amounts)
under $5.03 (1st percentile)
under $15.03 (10th percentile)

choices.reason: The policy gives no number. A label-free reading: an amount is small when it sits in the bottom 5% of what this bank's customers pay online (July to December 2016), which is $10.10; it is computed from the index at compile time, so the rule never learned from the case labels it is scored on. It also matches the agent's own card-testing detector (under $10), which keeps the rule-versus-agent comparison about structure, not about a dollar figure.

measured.what: 5th percentile of online transaction amounts before 2017

how.sql: select quantile_cont(TransactionAmt, 0.05) from txn where channel = ? and ts < ?

choices.question: Does 'within an hour' bound the small authorizations only, or also the larger purchase?

options.label: the small authorizations only
the whole sequence, larger purchase included

choices.reason: The comma reads 'Three or more small ... within an hour, followed by a larger purchase': the window phrase sits inside the first clause, before the comma, so it counts the tests; the cash-out is attached by 'followed by'.

choices.question: How soon after the last small authorization must the larger purchase come ('followed by')?

options.label: within 24 hours
within 1 hour
within 72 hours

choices.reason: The text sets no gap. R5's remedy is to decline pending authorizations and require step-up before further activity, which only makes sense while the cash-out is imminent; a day keeps it the same episode, and the episode builder's short lookback is 3 days (sensitivity shows 1 and 72 hours).

choices.question: How much larger is 'larger'?

options.label: not small: $10.10 or more (larger than every test by construction)
over 5 times the largest test and over $20 (the agent's bar)
over $100 (the rule's own block threshold)

choices.reason: 'larger' is a comparative and its referent is the small authorizations, so the literal reading is the opposite of small: any purchase at or above the small threshold is larger than every test. The agent's stricter bar (5 times and $20) and the rule's own $100 block threshold are measured as alternatives.

choices.question: What is an 'authorizations' in this data?

options.label: every transaction row (approved authorizations only are recorded)

choices.reason: The index has one row per approved transaction and no authorization or settlement status; declined test attempts are invisible, so the rule can only under-count tests. Recorded as a schema gap, no alternative is possible.

choices.question: Must the larger purchase also be online?

options.label: any channel
online only

choices.reason: 'online' qualifies the small authorizations; the larger purchase carries no channel word, so it is not restricted.

choices.question: What is 'one card' ('on one card')?

options.label: the card id of the alert
the account behind the card (holder_key, usable before 2017 only)

choices.reason: The card id is what the alert, the case and the answer name. In this data a card id pools many accounts (holder_key = card1, billing region and account start), so a pooled card can show three small online purchases in an hour from three different people; the account reading is measured as the alternative, but it cannot be the default because holder_key is unusable from January 2017 (D1 resampled, january-data-profile.md), the month under investigation.

choices.question: Which alerts does the rule fire for? The rule describes a sequence on a card, not one transaction.

options.label: a sequence within 72 hours either side of the flagged transaction
the flagged transaction is itself a test or the larger purchase
a sequence within 24 hours either side

choices.reason: R5 reacts to pending authorizations and to a purchase that has already cleared, i.e. to the card's activity around the alert, not to the flagged row alone. 72 hours equals the episode builder's short lookback (kavach.episode_model LOOKBACK_DAYS = 3).

choices.question: Which transactions may the rule see?

options.label: up to the case's opened_at (reference anchors: anchor + the median delay)

choices.reason: A detector may not use activity after the decision. Case anchors stop at opened_at; reference anchors, which have no case, stop at the anchor plus the median delay between a closed case's first fraudulent transaction and its opened_at, so both sides see the same amount of future on average.

choices.phrase: a purchase over $100 has already cleared
choices.question: What does 'already cleared' mean without a clearing status?

options.label: a purchase over $100 after the tests, at or before the decision time

choices.chosen: dated at or before the decision
choices.reason: The schema has no clearing status; a recorded transaction dated before the decision is treated as cleared (approved rows only are recorded).
